newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Latin America's other hostage drama drags on.
newsitem.headline: Latin America's other hostage drama drags on.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper applauded the stunning end to the hostage drama in Lima, saying he would have acted just as forcefully to restore law and order and win the release of victims of terror.

"Any head of state facing a situation of this kind, given that the rule of law was threatened as it was, would have acted in the same way," Samper told reporters late on Tuesday on the sidelines of an Andean summit in Bolivia.

What the embattled Colombian leader failed to mention is that a hostage drama in his own backyard is now well into its eighth month and there is no sign of it ending anytime soon. At least 60 soldiers were seized by Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas when they overran an army base in a remote area of southwest Colombia last Aug. 30.

Efforts to negotiate their release collapsed in December, due largely to mutual antagonisms and deep distrust between the military and the FARC's 70-year-old commander, Manuel Marulanda. Adding insult to injury, the FARC took 10 other troops hostage in January in northwestern Choco province.

Samper and senior military officials have bridled at suggestions that efforts to win the release of the captives, most of them poor conscripts no more than about 20 years old, have been put on the back burner. But their ordeal, in what FARC leaders call an "impenetrable" jungle fortress, contrasts sharply with the plight of the high-profile hostages including diplomats and business leaders rescued in Lima on Tuesday.
It is also one the world is more easily inclined to forget amid almost daily reports of kidnappings and murders in a country racked by seemingly uncontrolled violence.

Armed forces commander Gen. Harold Bedoya heralded the end to the Peru crisis by saying it showed how "the principle of authority" can be used "to resolve a complex and delicate problem" that pits "terrorists" against the state. He insisted Colombia's hostage drama was "completely different" from Peru's, however, since the soldiers are held somewhere in a vast jungle and not an embassy residence in the capital.

Local media reports soon after the FARC stormed the army base in Putumayo province, killing 36 soldiers, said the 150 men defending it had just 25 working rifles. Military leaders declined to comment on those reports.

But the attack marked the start of a nationwide guerrilla offensive in which scores of people were killed, prompting Western military experts to say the army had lost the momentum in Latin America's longest-running guerrilla war.

The FARC, which grew out of peasant militias formed in 1948, is the oldest and largest rebel group in Latin America. It has rejected recent peace overtures on grounds that Samper, who is alleged to have financed his 1994 campaign with drug money, heads an "illegitimate" government.
